controls.statement: A documented test strategy exists for the release's risk level.
Unit, component, integration, contract, system, end-to-end, smoke, and regression testing are included where appropriate.
Testing prioritizes critical and high-risk behavior rather than relying on aggregate code coverage.
Test data represents realistic size, shape, encoding, and edge conditions.
Personal and confidential test data is synthetic, masked, or properly authorized.
Release-gating tests are sufficiently deterministic.
Flaky tests are fixed or formally quarantined with a reviewed risk record.
Migration, upgrade, mixed-version, downgrade where supported, rollback, and roll-forward scenarios are tested.
Performance testing covers load, stress, spike, endurance, and capacity limits.
Security tests cover source, dependencies, deployed behavior, infrastructure, configuration, and business logic.
Critical calculations use independent verification or reconciliation.
Tests verify the exact artifact intended for production.
Independent penetration testing is completed where risk, contract, or regulation warrants it.
Define the unit or component boundary around cohesive behavior rather than arbitrary files or methods.
Test externally meaningful behavior and invariants rather than incidental implementation sequence.
Cover representative equivalence classes, boundaries, invalid inputs, state transitions, and error paths.
Test pure logic across all material branches and rules.
Test serialization, precision, time, locale, normalization, and identifier edge cases where relevant.
Control time, randomness, scheduling, environment, and external effects for determinism.
Use real domain values and builders that create valid data by default.
Keep each test independent and safe to run in any order and in parallel.
Make test names describe condition, behavior, and expected outcome.
Ensure assertions prove the intended behavior and fail when that behavior is broken.
Avoid excessive mocking that merely repeats implementation or permits impossible behavior.
Use contract-constrained fakes for external boundaries where appropriate.
Test resource cleanup, cancellation, retry, and idempotency locally where owned.
Use property-based, generative, mutation, or model-based testing for high-risk combinatorial logic.
Keep tests fast enough for frequent feedback without sacrificing meaningful coverage.
Measure critical behavior and mutation sensitivity rather than treating line coverage as the goal.
Refactor brittle tests when harmless internal change causes widespread failure.
Do not expose production internals solely to satisfy tests without a design benefit.
Review skipped, quarantined, or flaky tests with owner and expiry.
Convert escaped local defects into focused regression tests.
Identify every material internal and external boundary and its contract owner.
Test request, response, event, file, database, authentication, authorization, and error schemas.
Verify serialization, encoding, precision, ordering, pagination, null, optional, and unknown-field behavior.
Test provider and consumer expectations independently to support compatible evolution.
Run contract tests against faithful provider implementations or approved simulators.
Test persistence constraints, transactions, isolation, migrations, and query behavior using representative engines and settings.
Test authentication, authorization, tenant, quota, and rate behavior across boundaries.
Inject timeout, throttling, malformed, partial, duplicate, reordered, stale, and unavailable dependency responses.
Verify retry, idempotency, circuit breaking, fallback, reconciliation, and observability.
Test webhook signature, replay, ordering, retry, and duplicate delivery.
Test protocol and schema version negotiation and mixed-version operation.
Prevent shared mutable test environments from causing cross-test contamination.
Use isolated data and cleanup with evidence that cleanup cannot delete another test's resources.
Do not hide provider incompatibility behind mocks that are more permissive than reality.
Run a controlled subset against real third-party sandboxes or conformance endpoints where available.
Record provider version and configuration with results.
Monitor contract failures as release blockers for affected consumers.
Coordinate breaking changes through published migration and deprecation.
Test data residency, privacy, and logging at integration boundaries.
Convert production integration failures into reproducible contract cases.
Prioritize critical user and operator journeys by impact rather than attempting exhaustive UI-path enumeration.
Trace each acceptance test to approved requirements and business outcomes.
Use production-like topology, configuration, identity, data shape, integrations, and artifact builds.
Test onboarding, normal use, permission variation, recovery, cancellation, deletion, support, and administration as applicable.
Test alternate, error, degraded, offline, timeout, retry, and partial-success journeys.
Verify business invariants, notifications, background work, analytics, audit, and downstream effects.
Use multiple roles, tenants, accounts, locales, devices, browsers, and accessibility contexts.
Validate actual external boundaries where safe and use contract-tested substitutes otherwise.
Keep test setup and teardown deterministic, isolated, and observable.
Avoid making every detailed rule dependent on slow end-to-end tests.
Use stable semantic selectors and user-observable synchronization rather than implementation timing.
Record artifacts sufficient to diagnose failure across services.
Separate product acceptance from mere technical execution success.
Include support and operational acceptance for runbooks, monitoring, capacity, and recovery.
Verify data created, updated, exported, corrected, and deleted across all relevant stores.
Test deployment, mixed-version, migration, rollback, and post-deployment smoke behavior.
Manage flaky tests as defects with owner, cause, and expiry.
Run production-safe synthetic journeys for critical paths after launch.
Obtain qualified stakeholder acceptance for high-impact requirements.
Convert escaped journey defects into the lowest reliable regression layer plus an end-to-end sentinel when valuable.
Analyze change impact across requirements, modules, data, interfaces, consumers, dependencies, environments, and operations.
Select regression tests from risk and dependency evidence, not only changed files.
Maintain a stable critical regression suite that represents business, security, privacy, accessibility, and reliability invariants.
Test backward, forward, mixed-version, schema, protocol, browser, device, and data compatibility as applicable.
Test changed defaults, configuration, flags, permissions, quotas, and feature combinations.
Include known defect regressions and historically fragile areas.
Use differential or golden-master comparison carefully where behavior is large but not fully specified.
Review intended behavior changes so they do not appear as unexplained regression failures.
Run broad regression before irreversible or high-blast-radius changes.
Use production-representative data distributions and older valid records.
Test upgrades from every supported version and supported downgrade or roll-forward path.
Verify client and server caching does not preserve incompatible state.
Measure regression effectiveness through escaped defects and mutation or fault sensitivity.
Retire obsolete tests only after confirming the protected behavior or risk no longer exists.
Avoid allowing test-suite duration to grow without architecture and selection strategy.
Use staged test selection with mandatory high-risk gates and broader asynchronous evidence before final approval.
Verify the final artifact after packaging and deployment transformation.
Include security control and observability regression.
Preserve a known-good baseline and explain material differences.
Convert incidents caused by interaction effects into cross-component regression coverage.
Automate checks that are repeatable, valuable, and sufficiently deterministic.
Keep automation code to production-quality standards for review, versioning, security, and maintenance.
Make failures identify the violated expectation, actual result, context, and evidence.
Keep tests independent and safe for parallel or repeated execution.
Control time, randomness, external dependencies, and data where practical.
Use retries only to diagnose known infrastructure instability, never to convert flaky failures into passes.
Track flakiness, quarantine duration, ownership, and business risk.
Prevent test credentials, personal data, and secrets from leaking through fixtures and reports.
Version test data, simulators, schemas, baselines, and expected results with compatible production behavior.
Validate test tools and custom matchers against known passing and failing examples.
Ensure negative tests fail for the intended reason rather than an earlier setup problem.
Use layered tests to balance speed, fidelity, and diagnosis.
Avoid duplicated tests that add cost without new risk coverage.
Make environment and prerequisite failures distinct from product failures.
Preserve logs, traces, screenshots, videos, diffs, and seed values as appropriate.
Review disabled, skipped, expected-failure, and muted tests before release.
Measure suite duration, reliability, fault detection, maintenance cost, and escape rate.
Refactor automation when product implementation details make tests brittle.
Protect CI workers and test environments from untrusted code and cross-run contamination.
Periodically test that release gates actually block a deliberately failing change.
Define the production characteristics that each test environment must reproduce and those intentionally simulated.
Version infrastructure, configuration, schemas, dependencies, feature flags, and seed data.
Use synthetic data by default and authorize, minimize, mask, isolate, and expire production-derived data.
Preserve referential, statistical, temporal, locale, encoding, and edge-case characteristics needed for valid tests.
Include large, sparse, skewed, duplicate, malformed, legacy, deleted, and sensitive-shape records without exposing real identities.
Assign unique test identities, tenants, namespaces, and resources to prevent cross-run interference.
Prevent nonproduction notifications, payments, webhooks, and integrations from affecting real users or systems.
Use deterministic setup and teardown and detect orphaned resources.
Reset environments from reproducible automation rather than manual undocumented repair.
Detect drift between intended and actual environment configuration.
Protect test environments according to the sensitivity of code, credentials, and data they contain.
Keep production secrets and trust relationships out of lower environments.
Simulate dependency latency, error, throttling, and outage realistically.
Measure whether environment limitations invalidate test conclusions.
Maintain capacity sufficient for representative performance and concurrency tests.
Record environment version and health with every material result.
Prevent shared long-lived environments from hiding order dependence and contamination.
Test migration from realistic older schemas and data.
Review access and remove dormant test accounts, keys, data, and infrastructure.
Destroy or sanitize environments and data when their purpose ends.
Translate every material quality attribute into measurable scenarios with stimulus, environment, response, and threshold.
Use representative workloads, data, users, topology, dependencies, devices, and failure conditions.
Test latency distributions, throughput, saturation, resource use, and efficiency together.
Test availability and correctness under dependency, node, zone, network, storage, and control-plane failure.
Test recovery time, recovery point, data integrity, failover, failback, and restored operation.
Test security and privacy controls through adversarial and misuse scenarios.
Test accessibility through automation, keyboard, assistive technology, zoom, reflow, and human evaluation.
Test usability with representative tasks and users.
Test compatibility across supported clients, versions, formats, locales, and environments.
Test maintainability through change exercises, diagnostics, upgrade, and operator tasks where impact warrants it.
Test scalability and overload beyond expected peak to identify safe failure limits.
Test long-duration operation for leaks, drift, backlog, and degradation.
Test sustainability and cost under representative workload where material.
Verify monitoring and alerts during each quality test.
Record limitations, confidence, and conditions under which results do not apply.
Use independent review for high-impact thresholds and results.
Do not extrapolate beyond measured scale without an explicit model and uncertainty.
Repeat tests after material architecture, dependency, data, configuration, or infrastructure change.
Compare results to baselines and approved budgets.
Block release when a critical quality objective lacks valid evidence.
Prioritize charters by user harm, business impact, novelty, complexity, change, defect history, and uncertainty.
Define a mission and scope while preserving freedom to follow evidence.
Use skilled testers with domain, user, technical, accessibility, security, and operational context as appropriate.
Vary data, sequence, timing, concurrency, roles, devices, networks, locales, and interruption.
Investigate inconsistencies, ambiguous feedback, unexpected state, and recovery difficulty.
Explore complete workflows and cross-channel transitions rather than isolated screens.
Use heuristics, models, tours, personas, abuse stories, and past incidents to generate tests.
Capture concise notes, evidence, coverage, questions, risks, and follow-up.
Distinguish observations, hypotheses, defects, design concerns, and user research findings.
Reproduce and reduce defects to the smallest useful case.
Pair with developers, designers, support, operators, or users for high-context investigation.
Include users with disabilities and representative assistive technologies.
Avoid treating scripted checks as a replacement for exploration.
Time-box sessions and review whether additional exploration changes decisions.
Feed discoveries into requirements, automated regression, design, support, and risk records.
Track untested areas and session limitations.
Use production-like or production-safe environments without exposing real users or data.
Review quality across competing attributes rather than optimizing one path.
Measure escaped defect themes and charter effectiveness qualitatively.
Preserve psychological safety so testers can challenge accepted behavior.
Select techniques according to consequence, defect class, language semantics, and system complexity.

Capture affected user, journey, environment, version, data, time, symptoms, impact, and evidence.
Classify severity by harm, reach, integrity, security, privacy, financial, legal, and recoverability impact.
Separate severity from scheduling priority and make both explicit.
Triage duplicates without losing affected-user evidence or recurrence count.

Avoid stopping at individual error or a single proximate cause.

Review recurring low-severity defects whose aggregate burden is material.
